The problem

You come back to a project and ask “what was I doing?” The branch is there, but not why you were on it, what you had just tried, what was blocking you, or which files and pages mattered. Rebuilding that context quietly eats the first part of every session.

The idea

Clairn is named after a cairn, a stone marker that shows where a journey stopped. It preserves the context needed to resume a project: a short note on where you stopped, the next step, a blocker, the branch, and the files and tabs to reopen. It runs on your own computer.

2How someone actually uses it

Three moves. You save a stopping point when you leave, and you read it when you return.

Work as usual

Editor and terminal activity and the sites you choose are noticed on your computer. Nothing is uploaded.

$ git switch feature/retry
edit retry.ts
edit queue.ts
// still failing on timeout…

Save a stopping point

One command or shortcut saves a checkpoint: your note, the branch, the open files and cursor positions, and optionally your tabs.

$ clairn checkpoint "retry logic, half done"
Saved: 2 files, branch feature/retry
DocsSpecIssue

Come back and resume

Open Clairn and the Resume card shows where you stopped and what to do first. Restore reopens your files and tabs after a preview.
